         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”)1, Clean Energy Advocates2 and

Community Organizations3 respectfully submit this protest in response to the October 2, 2026

docket, which proposes revisions to MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating

Reserve Markets Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”)

process.4 For the reasons explained below, the Commission should reject the LARS proposal.

      I.   Introduction

          As the Commission has recognized, integrated planning processes can help ensure that

generation and transmission can be arranged to supply nearby large customers reliably, at lower

cost, and with faster engineering study processes, ultimately resulting in more just and

reasonable rates without harming other existing or future customers or suppliers. Better load and

generation interconnection processes are clearly needed. MISO’s LARS proposal does not

achieve that end, nor does it improve other interconnection processes. Instead of improving the

coordination of generation and transmission planning, MISO’s LARS proposal is a new,

permanent parallel interconnection study process that will shift costs from large loads to other

existing and future transmission customers and resource owners, create and worsen reliability

concerns, and allow for unchecked and harmful anti-competitive discrimination. The

Commission should reject LARS because it is not just and reasonable and is unduly

discriminatory or, in the alternative, issue a deficiency letter requiring MISO to demonstrate how

LARS can be made just and reasonable.


    II.   Background

              A. Large Load Growth and Interconnection

          MISO estimates that annual load growth will be 1 to 3 percent per year from 2025

through 2044.5 MISO integrates new generation and load through separate processes on different

schedules.6 New generation enters either through MISO’s cluster-based Definitive Planning

Phase (“DPP”) or its temporary, serialized Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”). The

DPP operates on a 365-day timeline and ERAS operates quarterly. New load is accounted for

 through the MISO Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”) or the Expedited Project Review

(“EPR”). Where MTEP operates on an 18-month cycle, EPR provides approval in roughly 90

days. MISO acknowledges that “large loads have overtaken the EPR process.”7 The 89 EPR

requests approved in MTEP26 accounted for roughly 54 percent of the approximately $14.7

billion of transmission investment approved in that cycle.8

       A generator may be treated as an alternative to a transmission solution only once that

generator has a signed interconnection agreement (“GIA”).9 This poses a timing problem. A

large load whose transmission solution depends on a new generator cannot obtain MTEP

approval until the generator has completed the DPP or ERAS interconnection queues. MISO

describes this “timing problem” as the problem the LARS parallel study process is designed to

solve.10

           B. The Show Cause Order

       On June 18, 2026, the Commission instituted a proceeding under section 206 of the

Federal Power Act (“the Act” or “FPA”), preliminarily finding that MISO’s Tariff “appears to be

unjust and unreasonable because it lacks provisions that address, with sufficient clarity and

consistency, how MISO and/or the Transmission Owners will timely study . . . the provision of

transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads.”11 The Commission directed

MISO to show cause why the Tariff remains just and reasonable without provisions addressing

                    1. Study procedures for large loads

         The Commission found that the Tariff lacks “sufficiently clear and consistent provisions

regarding the study process” for large loads, pointing to the “ad hoc study process” reflected in

Transmission Owner study agreements “not reflected in MISO’s Tariff,” and identified the

elements such provisions should contain. These include:

             (1) A definition of large load.

             (2) A rolling application process with non-refundable fees, escalating readiness

                requirements, and disclosure of duplicative requests.

             (3) Study procedures that account for large-load behavior and flexibility.

             (4) Evaluations of alternative transmission technologies “in all instances,” with a

                written demonstration whenever traditional Network Upgrades are selected

                instead.

             (5) A 60-to-90-day study deadline.

             (6) Ongoing operational requirements.

                   2. Cost shifting

       The Commission found that the Tariff “appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it

lacks adequate mechanisms to mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers,”

and identified two remedies. First, public posting of the Network Upgrades needed to serve large

loads and their costs.14 Second, a pro forma cost recovery agreement requiring the Eligible

Customer to make “a minimum contribution toward the transmission owner’s transmission

revenue requirement,” sized to the megawatts of service requested and secured by credit support,

so that large-load-driven costs are not “paid by other transmission customers that neither caused

the need for nor benefit commensurately from those Network Upgrades.”15

                   3. Generation serving electrically proximate load

       The Commission defined an “electrically proximate large load” as one “sufficiently

electrically close to the interconnection customer’s requested point of interconnection” that the

combined impact of generator and load “will be effectively the same as if they were located at

the same substation (e.g., large load that is located no more than two substations away from the

generating facility),” and invited revisions “appropriately tailored to MISO’s transmission

system.”16 It found that MISO’s Tariff is deficient because it lacks a study process or

interconnection service that reflects “an interconnection customer’s commitment in an

interconnection agreement to limit the generating facility’s output” while serving such a load.17

        Referencing SPP’s High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”)

process, the Commission stated that such a generator’s interconnection service “should be of an

interim nature until the interconnection customer obtains” Energy Resource Interconnection

Service (“ERIS”) or Network Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”), and noted that

MISO’s system “may warrant consideration of a more limited definition of electrically

proximate.”18 The Commission directed that any responsive filing to the Show Cause Order

address whether such generators would participate in MISO’s energy, ancillary services, and

capacity markets, with what restrictions, and how they would be accredited.19

       The Commission “strongly encourage[d]” MISO to address these directives through

filings under section 205, but specified that any such filing “should also explain which of the

Commission’s above directives their filing addresses and how it resolves them.”20

           C. The LARS Proposal

       On October 2, 2026, MISO filed proposed revisions to Attachment X (the Generator

Interconnection Procedures, or “GIP”), Appendices 1 and 6 to Attachment X, and Attachment FF

to establish the Large Load Addition Resource Study, with a requested effective date of

December 2, 2026 and a first study period in the first quarter of 2027.21 MISO described LARS

as “expedited review of the addition of 200 MW or greater loads together with new generation

resources that are electrically proximate to those loads,” conducted in a parallel study process

lasting up to 120 days that builds on EPR and ERAS.22 Unlike ERAS, however, LARS “will be a

permanent MISO study process.”23

        LARS creates at least two major changes to how generation interconnection and

transmission planning function in MISO. First, LARS creates an exception to the EPR

requirement described above in which a generator can be considered an alternative transmission

solution only after it has a GIA. Under MISO’s proposed process, a generator that has submitted

a valid LARS application and holds a five-year or longer contract (e.g., Power Purchase

Agreement or similar off-take agreement) with the large load “may be considered as an

alternative transmission solution” in the load study even though it does not have a GIA.24

Second, the proposed process creates a new, 120-day serial generator interconnection track

outside of the DPP and ERAS, through which the paired generator receives NRIS under a new

form of agreement called the Large Load Generator Interconnection Agreement (“LLGIA”).25

MISO presents LARS as responsive to the Show Cause Order’s electrically proximate directive

and resource adequacy concerns, and as independent of “[t]he cost shifting issues raised in the

Commission’s Show Cause Order,” which “will be addressed in future filings.”26

       Four entities drive the LARS process. Only the entity that procures transmission service

for a large load may initiate and submit a LARS Application.27 This entity is called a “LARS

Associated Transmission Customer,” which MISO states is often a Load Serving Entity

(“LSE”).28 MISO’s proposal does not set any criteria, timelines, or disclosure obligations on a

LARS Associated Transmission Customer’s decision whether to sponsor a particular generator

and load. A generator-load pair, however, has no path into LARS without such sponsorship.29

           D. The Stakeholder Process

       MISO developed LARS in eleven weeks. It first presented the concept to its Large Load

Working Group (“LLWG”) on July 16, 2026.55 After presenting revisions at different meetings,

MISO presented final language on September 23 and filed on October 2.56

       Stakeholders raised, and MISO declined to address, several of the concerns presented in

this protest. The Environmental Sector objected to the Transmission Customer’s gatekeeping

role, to the LRZ-wide scope of the pairing requirement, and to LARS’s failure to meet the Show

Cause Order’s electrically proximate standard, and asked that generators and loads be jointly

liable for upgrade costs if a pairing ends early. Energy Futures Group presented the Generator

and Load Interconnection Process (“GALIP”), which would study large loads and their

generation together within the DPP, with full cost-causation-based allocation of upgrade costs

and both firm and non-firm service options for load.57 MISO declined to pursue GALIP, stating

that it “does not believe in a ‘one size fits all’ approach to interconnection” and that GALIP

“aimed to shoehorn a parallel generation/load study process into the existing DPP process.”58

 III.    Arguments

            A. LARS creates a cost shift from large loads and their generation to other
               customers

        It is a long-standing principle of Commission ratemaking that “all approved rates reflect

to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them,” and that

compliance is measured “by comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed

or benefits drawn by that party.”59 In the Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily

found that MISO’s Tariff violates that principle because it “lacks adequate mechanisms to

mitigate the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers” when large loads drive network

upgrades.60 LARS does not supply those mechanisms. By MISO’s own account, LARS adopts

no cost allocation methodology, and “[t]he cost shifting issues raised in the Commission’s Show

Cause Order will be addressed in future filings.”61

        Instead, LARS builds cost shifting into the process in four ways. First, it assigns the

network upgrades that a generator-load pair requires to the transmission pricing zone rather than

to the pair. Second, it studies LARS generators in models that exclude the DPP queue, and

resolves the resulting double-allocation of transmission capacity through MTEP projects paid for

by zonal load and through curtailment of DPP generators that paid for their own upgrades. Third,

it allows either half of a pair to leave the system after fifteen years and the generator to fail at any

time, leaving zonal load to pay for whatever transmission must then be built. Fourth, it defers the

cost recovery agreement, financial security, and transparency measures the Commission

identified as necessary. The Commission should reject LARS or, at a minimum, decline to make

                   1. LARS assigns upgrade costs to the pricing zone

       As explained above, LARS sorts network upgrades identified in its load and generation

studies into three categories: violations in only the load study, violations in only the generation

study, and violations in both studies. Violations that occur only in the load study or in both the

load and generation studies are assigned the BRP or Other project types and their costs are

allocated to all loads in the Transmission Owner’s pricing zone. Only when a violation occurs in

the generation study alone will MISO assign the costs of the mitigations to the Interconnection

Customer as a GIP upgrade.62 MISO calls this a “cost allocation hierarchy—transitioning from

GIP to BRP when appropriate.”63 This hierarchy represents impermissible cost shifts.

       When the costs of mitigation are assigned to BRP or Other project types, those costs are

allocated to the Transmission Owner in whose pricing zone the project is located. Those costs are

then recovered through the Transmission Owner’s rates, paid for by every transmission customer

in the zone. MISO explains that the costs will fall on “the load within the transmission pricing

zone where the transmission upgrade is required.”64 In contrast, when the same generator

interconnects through the DPP, the Interconnection Customer funds the Network Upgrades its

interconnection requires. LARS, therefore, takes a category of costs usually assigned to

generators and assigns them to existing load. It is not as though the beneficiaries are unknown or

diffuse. Rather, the beneficiaries are simply the generator and the large load, for which the

generator is the “alternative transmission solution.”65 MISO has failed to show how the LBA or

          LARS is likely to shift the cumulative upgrades needed to support the transmission

system, because of the serialized LARS study process. Each LARS generator is studied

“individually in a serial fashion” in its own model.66 Unlike a DPP cluster study, which identifies

the upgrades a group of generators needs together and allocates their costs among the cluster, the

LARS generation study never captures the combined effect of the ten generators and loads in a

study period, let alone of the thirty pairs that may enter LARS each year. In fact, constraints that

emerge from the cumulative injection of LARS generators or cumulative impacts of LARS large

loads are most likely to appear in a load study where all ten pairs are studied together. In that

case, however, as explained above, those mitigations will be classified as BRP or Other.

Otherwise, the problems will reveal themselves in a later MTEP study. Either way, costs will be

allocated not to the load-generation pair, but to all load in the zone.

          The pricing zone that pays for upgrades caused by LARS projects may not even be the

LBA in which the LARS Associated Load takes service. While load-generation pairs must be in

the same LRZ, MISO studies “the full impacts of the generation/load pair on MISO’s

Transmission system” without confining the study to that zone.67 A single LRZ can span

multiple LBAs, Transmission Owner pricing zones, and states. Because MISO declined to limit

the generation/load pairs to a single LBA or to a set number of substations, the result is that

customers of one Transmission Owner, in one state, can be assigned the cost of upgrades

The state regulator responsible for protecting those customers has no jurisdiction over the load

        Transmission upgrade costs associated with LARS generation should not be assigned to

load generally, because both the driver and the beneficiaries of the upgrade are a specific

generator-load pair.70 The NRIS service for a LARS Interconnection Customer hinges on the

consumption of the LARS associated load. MISO acknowledges this tight connection by

terminating the LLGIA, and sending the generator back to the DPP for new interconnection

service if the load leaves or shrinks within fifteen years.71 A generator whose interconnection

service is contingent on one load’s consumption is not a system resource whose upgrades benefit

the zone.

                    1. Parallel independent studies produce unreliable results and reliability risks

       Interconnection studies assign network upgrades on the basis of cumulative impacts. By

putting some generators in one model and other generators in another, MISO cannot capture

those impacts. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation’s (“NERC”) model

validation guidance states that future-year planning cases “should contain the same component

representations as the most recently validated model, unless there is a specific reason for the data

to be different,” and should represent “the cumulative planned changes to the system” through

the period studied.152 By excluding the DPP, LARS does the opposite of NERC’s procedures.

Neither set of studies sees the other until MTEP, which is after LLGIAs have been executed and

DPP customers have been assigned their upgrades.

       The consequences of this mutual blindness of the models are not limited to the cost shifts

described above. A constraint that appears only when the two sets of projects are combined

might be a contingency for which no mitigation was identified and no upgrade was built, leaving

real-time operators without the reconfiguration options the planning process assumed. In the

worst case, cascading blackouts could result. A more moderate negative outcome might be load

shed as the only tool available to manage unstudied conditions. MISO does not appear to

describe the dispatch and case assumptions for the LARS load study. MTEP-based load studies

and DPP interconnection studies in MISO are built on different cases and different dispatch

assumptions. Without an explanation of which assumptions LARS will use, the Commission has

no basis to find that a load study built upon MISO’s existing EPR process will identify the

constraints that a DPP study of the same generator would identify.
